title: Two little shrines at Kamo
translation: At the Kamo Shrine there are two small shrines, Iwamoto and Hashimoto. Iwamoto is for Narihira, and Hashimoto is for Sanekata. People always mix them up, so one year when I was there, I stopped an old shrine official who was walking past and asked him.
"Sanekata is the one whose reflection was seen in the shrine's stream, they say," he told me, "so I'd think it's Hashimoto, since that one is nearer the water. And Abbot Jien wrote:

The gentle man of old
who loved the moon
and gazed at the blossoms:
here he is,
Ariwara.
I've always been told he wrote it at the Iwamoto shrine. But you probably know far better than people like us." He said it so respectfully. I was very impressed.

Lady Konoe, who served Imadegawa-in and has a great many poems in the anthologies, used to write sets of a hundred poems when she was young and offer them at those two shrines, written in water. She really was highly regarded, and plenty of her poems are still quoted. She also wrote Chinese poems and their prefaces beautifully.

literal: Iwamoto and Hashimoto at Kamo are Narihira and Sanekata.

Since people always confuse them, one year when I went there, I called to an old shrine official who was passing and asked him, and (he said): 'Since Sanekata is said to be the one whose reflection appeared in the purifying stream, I think it must be Hashimoto, since it is still nearer the water.
'The gentle man of old who loved the moon and gazed at the blossoms is here: Ariwara'
composed (this), and I have heard that it was at the Iwamoto shrine, but you may well know better than people like us', he said very respectfully, and that seemed splendid to me.

The person called Konoe of Imadegawa-in, who is included many times in the anthologies, when she was young, always composed hundred-poem sets and offered them before those two shrines, writing them in water.
Truly she had a high reputation, and many of her poems are on people's lips.
She is a person who writes Chinese poems, prefaces to poems and the like splendidly.

notes.text: Two small subsidiary shrines of the Upper Kamo Shrine in Kyoto. Ariwara no Narihira (825–880) and Fujiwara no Sanekata (died 998) were both poets, and both were famous as lovers.

notes.quote: 御手洗に影のうつりける
notes.text: {御手洗|みたらし}: the stream at the shrine where visitors purify themselves. The official refers to a story that Sanekata's reflection was seen in it; the details of the story are not certain.
Jien (1155–1225), four times head of the Tendai school, a major poet and the author of a history of Japan, the Gukanshō. Yoshimizu was where he lived.
A pun: ここにあり 'is here' runs straight into Ariwara, Narihira's family name. The poem names him without naming him.

notes.quote: 御存じなどもこそさぶらはめ
notes.text: もこそ … め: 'you may well (know)'. さぶらふ is polite. The official gives his answer and then politely hands the question back to the visitor.
こそ … しか: こそ needs the realis form, so き becomes しか. Kenkō was there himself.

A lady-in-waiting called Konoe, who served Imadegawa-in (Saionji Kishi, consort of Emperor Kameyama). She was a respected poet of the late thirteenth century, with many poems in the imperial anthologies ({集|しふ}).

notes.quote: 水にて書きて手向けられけり
notes.text: {手向|たむ}く: to offer to the gods. Poems written in water leave no trace for human readers; commentators usually take this as an offering meant for the gods alone.
{作文|さくもん}: Chinese poetry (see section 1). {詩序|しじよ}: a prose preface to a set of Chinese poems. Few women at court wrote in Chinese.
